blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 22 (Hydroxy Compounds), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 What are alcohols? Describe their classification (i) by the number of hydroxyl groups and (ii) by the type of carbon atom carrying the -OH group, with general formulae and examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Alcohols are hydroxy compounds whose functional group is the hydroxyl group (-OH), attached to an aliphatic carbon. General formula ROH, where R is an alkyl group. Methanol (CH₃OH) and ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) are the first two members of the monohydric series; cholesterol and the carbohydrates also belong to the family.

(i) By the number of -OH groups:
• Monohydric alcohols: one -OH group, e.g. ethanol, propan-1-ol.
• Polyhydric alcohols: more than one -OH group, e.g. glycol (1,2-ethanediol, two -OH) and glycerol (1,2,3-propanetriol, three -OH).

(ii) By the number of carbon atoms directly attached to the carbon bonded to -OH:
• Primary (1°): -OH on a primary carbon; general formula R₁CH₂OH, e.g. propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
• Secondary (2°): -OH on a secondary carbon; R₂CHOH, e.g. propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.
• Tertiary (3°): -OH on a tertiary carbon; R₃COH, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH.

book_ref.quote: Depending on the number of carbon atoms which are directly attached to the carbon that is bonded with the -OH group, alcohols can be classified into three types.

blocks.prompt: 2 Write the dissociation equilibria of an alcohol and of water. Explain the meaning of a low degree of dissociation and how the positive inductive effect of the alkyl group affects the alkoxide ion. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Equilibria:
ROH(aq) ⇌ RO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq)
H₂O(l) ⇌ OH⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq)

Low degree of dissociation: when dissolved in water, alcohol molecules split up into ions only to a small extent. The equilibrium lies far to the left, so there are many more ROH molecules than RO⁻ and H⁺ ions. Water's equilibrium also lies to the left, but it gives more H⁺ ions. Since alcohols have a lower [H⁺(aq)] than water, they are weaker acids than water.

Role of the alkyl group:
• Alkyl groups are electron donating; they push electrons into a covalent bond (positive inductive effect).
• Removing H⁺ from the alcohol gives the alkoxide ion, e.g. CH₃CH₂O⁻ (ethoxide). Its O atom is bonded to the electron-donating alkyl group, so there is more electron density on O.
• This destabilises the alkoxide ion; it is more likely to accept an H⁺ ion and form the alcohol again. Hence the alcohol ionises less and is less acidic than water.

book_ref.quote: The reason for alcohols being less acidic than water is the presence of alkyl groups.

blocks.prompt: 3 Compare the conjugate bases of phenol and ethanol. Use the comparison to place phenol, water and ethanol in order of acidity. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Phenol loses H⁺ to give the phenoxide ion, C₆H₅O⁻; ethanol loses H⁺ to give the ethoxide ion, CH₃CH₂O⁻. The stability of each conjugate base decides how easily the proton is lost.

Order of acidity: phenol > water > ethanol.

book_ref.quote: Although phenol compounds contain an alcohol (-OH) group, they are weakly acidic and this is due to the delocalisation of one of the lone pairs from the oxygen atom into the aromatic ring.

rows: One lone pair on O overlaps with the delocalised π system of the ring
O is bonded to an electron-donating alkyl group (positive inductive effect)
Negative charge spread over the ring; less charge density on O
Ion stabilised; H⁺ not strongly attracted, less likely to re-form phenol
Ion destabilised; readily accepts H⁺ and re-forms ethanol
Phenol more likely to lose a proton: more acidic than water
Ethanol ionises little: less acidic than water

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the preparation of alcohols from alkenes (two methods) and from halogenoalkanes, giving reagents, conditions, equations and the type of reaction. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Alkene + steam (hydration): hot steam is reacted with the alkene using concentrated phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) as catalyst. Electrophilic addition takes place.
CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH (ethene to ethanol)

2. Oxidation of alkenes with cold, dilute KMnO₄: this mild oxidising agent converts the alkene into a diol (two -OH groups).
CH₂=CH₂ + [O] + H₂O → HOCH₂–CH₂OH (ethene to 1,2-ethanediol)

3. From halogenoalkanes: the halogen atom is substituted by -OH when the halogenoalkane is heated with aqueous NaOH. This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction.
CH₃CH₂Br + NaOH(aq) → CH₃CH₂OH + NaBr (bromoethane to ethanol)

book_ref.quote: When hot steam is reacted with an alkene, using concentrated phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) as a catalyst, electrophilic addition takes place to form an alcohol.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe how alcohols are obtained from aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and esters. State the class of alcohol formed in each reduction. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Aldehydes: reduced by NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ to primary alcohols.
CH₃CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂OH (ethanal to ethanol)

2. Ketones: reduced by NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ to secondary alcohols.
CH₃COCH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (propanone to propan-2-ol)

3. Carboxylic acids: reduced by LiAlH₄ to primary alcohols, e.g. ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, to ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH.

4. Esters: heated with dilute acid, hydrolysis takes place and a carboxylic acid and an alcohol are formed.
CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH (ethyl ethanoate to ethanoic acid and ethanol)

book_ref.quote: Aldehydes and ketones can be reduced by reducing agents such as NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ to obtain alcohols.

blocks.prompt: 6 Ethene reacts with hot steam over concentrated H₃PO₄: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH. Calculate the mass of ethanol formed and the mass of steam used when 14 g of ethene reacts completely. (Molar masses: ethene 28, water 18, ethanol 46 g mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert grams of ethene to moles; the equation is 1 : 1 : 1, so moles of steam and ethanol are the same; convert back to grams.

book_ref.quote: i) Ethene and steam to ethanol

steps: Mole ratio ethene : H₂O : ethanol = 1 : 1 : 1, so H₂O used = 0.50 mol and ethanol formed = 0.50 mol
blocks.final_answer: Ethanol formed = 23 g; steam used = 9.0 g

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the combustion, substitution and dehydration reactions of ethanol, giving equations, reagents and the type of reaction in each case. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Combustion: when ignited, alcohols undergo complete combustion to carbon dioxide and water.
CH₃CH₂OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O, ΔH°c = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹
The reaction is highly exothermic, so ethanol is used as an alternative to petrol in some countries.

2. Substitution: the -OH group is replaced by another substituent such as a halogen, giving a halogenoalkane.
CH₃CH₂OH + HCl → CH₃CH₂Cl + H₂O (ZnCl₂)

3. Dehydration: an elimination reaction in which a water molecule is removed and an alkene is formed. Dehydrating agents: aluminium oxide, conc. sulphuric acid, conc. phosphoric acid.
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O

book_ref.quote: Alcohols when ignited, undergo complete combustion to form carbon dioxide and water.

blocks.prompt: 8 The standard enthalpy of combustion of ethanol is −1367 kJ mol⁻¹ (CH₃CH₂OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O). Calculate (i) the heat released when 9.2 g of ethanol burns completely and (ii) the mass of CO₂ produced. (Molar masses: ethanol 46, CO₂ 44 g mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find moles of ethanol; heat = moles × 1367 kJ; CO₂ moles are twice ethanol moles from the equation.

book_ref.quote: The above reaction is highly exothermic; this is why the alcohol is used as an alternate to petrol in some countries.

blocks.final_answer: (i) 273.4 kJ of heat released; (ii) 17.6 g of CO₂

blocks.prompt: 9 A burner must supply 2050.5 kJ of heat by burning ethanol (ΔH°c = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹; CH₃CH₂OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O). Calculate the mass of ethanol needed and the volume of oxygen used at STP. (Molar mass of ethanol 46 g mol⁻¹; molar volume of a gas at STP 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Moles of ethanol = heat needed ÷ heat per mole; then use the 1 : 3 ratio for oxygen.

book_ref.quote: Alcohols when ignited, undergo complete combustion to form carbon dioxide and water.

steps: Volume of O₂ at STP = 4.5 × 22.4 = 100.8 dm³
blocks.final_answer: 69 g of ethanol; 100.8 dm³ of O₂ at STP

blocks.prompt: 10 Describe the reaction of ethanol with sodium metal. How is it used as a test for the -OH group, and how does it compare with the reaction of sodium with water and with longer-chain alcohols? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reaction: the O-H bond of the hydroxyl group breaks; hydrogen gas is given off and a base, the alkoxide, is formed.
2CH₃CH₂OH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂ONa + H₂(g)
If the excess ethanol is evaporated, a white crystalline solid of sodium ethoxide is left.

Test for -OH: bubbles of hydrogen gas are released when sodium is added if a hydroxy group is present.

Comparison with water: the reaction is less vigorous than that of sodium with water. With phenolphthalein, sodium in ethanol gives the pink colour slowly, while in water the pink colour appears immediately.

Chain length: the longer the hydrocarbon chain of the alcohol, the less vigorous the reaction becomes.

book_ref.quote: When an alcohol reacts with a reactive metal such as sodium (Na), the oxygen-hydrogen bond in the hydroxly group breaks.

blocks.prompt: 11 4.6 g of ethanol reacts completely with excess sodium: 2CH₃CH₂OH + 2Na → 2CH₃CH₂ONa + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen at STP and the mass of sodium ethoxide left after evaporating the excess ethanol. (Molar masses: ethanol 46, sodium ethoxide 68 g mol⁻¹; molar volume at STP 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Moles of ethanol give equal moles of sodium ethoxide and half as many moles of H₂.

book_ref.quote: If the excess ethanol is evaporated off after the reaction, a white crystalline solid of sodium alkoxide is left.

steps: Volume of H₂ at STP = 0.050 × 22.4 = 1.12 dm³
Moles of CH₃CH₂ONa = 0.10 mol; mass = 0.10 × 68 = 6.8 g
blocks.final_answer: 1.12 dm³ of H₂ at STP; 6.8 g of sodium ethoxide

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe the oxidation of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Explain the colour change, the need for the acid, and how the reaction distinguishes tertiary alcohols. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Oxidising agents for alcohols include acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (potassium dichromate(VI), orange) and acidified KMnO₄.

• Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes: CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O (ethanol to ethanal).
• Secondary alcohols are oxidised only to ketones (on heating): CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O (propan-2-ol to propanone).
• Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation.

Colour change: when an alcohol is oxidised, the orange dichromate ions (Cr₂O₇²⁻) are reduced to green Cr³⁺ ions.

Need for acid: to act as an oxidising agent the dichromate must itself be reduced; this reduction requires H⁺ ions, provided by the acidic medium.

Test: propan-1-ol (primary) and propan-2-ol (secondary) turn the orange solution green; 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary) shows no colour change. So the test shows a primary or secondary alcohol is present.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, only the oxidation of primary and secondary alcohols will change the colour of acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ solution

blocks.prompt: 13 In the preparation of phenol from phenylamine, explain the purpose of: (i) making nitrous acid in situ from NaNO₂ and HCl (ii) using ice to keep the mixture below 10°C (iii) warming in the final step (iv) the reagent used in the final step. Give the equations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Phenols can be produced from phenylamine and nitrous acid (HNO₂) in three steps.

(i) HNO₂ is so unstable that it cannot be kept; it is made in the test-tube when needed: NaNO₂ + HCl → HNO₂ + NaCl.

(ii) The temperature is kept below 10°C with ice because HNO₂ is unstable, and the diazonium salt formed from phenylamine is also unstable:
C₆H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O

(iii) On further warming, the diazonium salt is decomposed (hydrolysed) and phenol is produced with nitrogen gas:
C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl

(iv) Water: warming the diazonium salt solution with water hydrolyses it to phenol (equation in iii). The book's 22.5 scheme prints NaOH here, which is not correct (Book correction).

book_ref.quote: The HNO₂ is so unstable that it needs to be prepared in a test-tube by reacting sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) and dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) while keeping the temperature below 10°C using ice.

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the reactions of the -OH group of phenol with (i) sodium hydroxide (ii) sodium metal (iii) ethanoyl chloride, giving balanced equations and the role of the base in (iii). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The -OH group of phenol is slightly acidic, so phenol takes part in acid-base reactions.

(i) With bases: phenol is only slightly soluble in water (large non-polar ring) but dissolves in alkali, forming a soluble salt and water.
C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O

(ii) With reactive metals: molten phenol reacts vigorously with sodium; a soluble salt forms and hydrogen gas is given off.
2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂

(iii) With an acyl chloride: phenol heated with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of a base gives the ester phenyl ethanoate.
CH₃COCl + C₆H₅OH → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl
Role of the base: it deprotonates phenol to the phenoxide ion (C₆H₅OH + OH⁻ → C₆H₅O⁻ + H₂O). The phenoxide ion is a better nucleophile than phenol and attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethanoyl chloride.

book_ref.quote: The -OH group in phenols has a slightly acidic character It can therefore act as an acid and take part in acid-base reactions.

blocks.prompt: 15 18.8 g of molten phenol reacts completely with sodium: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂. Calculate (i) the mass of sodium used (ii) the mass of sodium phenoxide formed (iii) the volume of hydrogen at STP. (Molar masses: phenol 94, Na 23, sodium phenoxide 116 g mol⁻¹; molar volume at STP 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Phenol, Na and sodium phenoxide are in a 1 : 1 : 1 ratio; H₂ is half the moles of phenol.

book_ref.quote: Now, a soluble salt is formed and hydrogen gas is given off.

steps: Moles of Na = 0.20 mol; mass of Na = 0.20 × 23 = 4.6 g
Moles of C₆H₅ONa = 0.20 mol; mass = 0.20 × 116 = 23.2 g
Moles of H₂ = 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10 mol; volume at STP = 0.10 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³
blocks.final_answer: (i) 4.6 g Na (ii) 23.2 g sodium phenoxide (iii) 2.24 dm³ H₂ at STP

blocks.prompt: 16 Explain how the -OH group activates the benzene ring of phenol and where it directs electrophiles. Describe the bromination of phenol with its observation and equation, and contrast it with the bromination of benzene. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Activation: the oxygen atom of the -OH group donates electron density into the ring. One of its lone pairs overlaps with the π system of the benzene ring and becomes delocalised, increasing the electron density of the ring. The ring is therefore more likely to undergo electrophilic attack (it is activated). Incoming electrophiles are directed to the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

Bromination of phenol: phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature, without a catalyst, in an electrophilic substitution. The orange bromine solution is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms.
C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr

Benzene: undergoes bromination only with pure bromine (not a solution) in the presence of anhydrous aluminium bromide (AlBr₃) catalyst at room temperature. Phenol, being activated, reacts readily with bromine water in the absence of a catalyst.

book_ref.quote: One of the lone pairs of the oxygen atom overlaps with the π system of the benzene ring and becomes delocalised, causing an increased electron density in the aromatic ring.

blocks.prompt: 17 Excess bromine water is added to a solution containing 4.7 g of phenol: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr. Calculate the mass of bromine that reacts and the mass of white precipitate formed. (Molar masses: phenol 94, Br₂ 160, 2,4,6-tribromophenol 331 g mol⁻¹.) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Phenol is the limiting reactant; each mole uses 3 mol Br₂ and gives 1 mol of 2,4,6-tribromophenol (the white precipitate).

book_ref.quote: Phenols also undergo electrophilic substitution reactions when reacted with bromine water at room temperature.

steps: Moles of Br₂ reacting = 3 × 0.050 = 0.15 mol; mass = 0.15 × 160 = 24 g
blocks.final_answer: 24 g of Br₂ reacts; about 16.6 g of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms

blocks.prompt: 18 What is a phenolic compound? Explain, with 1-naphthol as the example, how the -OH group affects the reactivity of the naphthalene ring and where electrophiles attack. How does 1-naphthol behave towards bromine water? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Phenolic compounds are compounds other than phenol (C₆H₅OH) in which a hydroxyl group is bonded to an aromatic ring; 1-naphthol and 2-naphthol are examples.

• 1-naphthol contains a hydroxy group attached to position 1 of naphthalene.
• Just as in phenol, the -OH group is electron-donating: a lone pair on O is delocalised into the ring, so the naphthalene ring is activated towards electrophilic substitution.
• Electrophiles are directed to the 2 and/or 4 positions.
• 1-naphthol and other phenolic compounds react in a similar way to phenol; for example, 1-naphthol undergoes bromination with bromine water, the bromine entering the activated 2 and/or 4 positions.

book_ref.quote: 1-naphthol and other phenolic compounds react in a similar way as phenol.

blocks.prompt: 19 Compare ethanol and phenol in a table: where the -OH group is attached, acidity relative to water, reaction with sodium, reaction with bromine water, and one method of preparation. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Both are hydroxy compounds, but in phenol both the polar OH group and the electron-rich ring react:

book_ref.quote: Phenols can undergo many types of reactions as both the electron-rich benzene ring and the polar OH group can participate in chemical reactions.

rows: Less acidic than water (alkyl group destabilises ethoxide)
More acidic than water (phenoxide stabilised by delocalisation)
No ring, so no substitution with bromine water
Decolourises bromine water; white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol
Prepared from ethene + steam (conc. H₃PO₄ catalyst)
Prepared from phenylamine + HNO₂ via the diazonium salt
